body:
Tuesday night was fun. Tonight’s show, however, was maybe even more important.
If you watched our livestream Tuesday night as we wargamed the Cornyn collapse in real-time, you already know what happened: the Paxton positions exploded, the margin market went nuclear, and one of the trades we highlighted at around 8 cents wound up paying out for over a 1000% gain.
That’s the flashy part. 
Tonight’s episode of 
Predictable
 was about something much more valuable: How we got there 
before
 the market fully understood what was happening.
Because honestly, anyone can celebrate a result after the fact. The entire point of this show is figuring out 
why
 the market is mispricing something while there’s still time to act on it. That’s what we walked through tonight. Not just “Paxton won” but also why the market kept underestimating the size of the win. Why the Trump endorsement changed the race more than traders wanted to admit. Why the margin markets were still sleepy even after the outright winner market had mostly corrected itself.
And maybe most importantly: Why prediction markets keep revealing signals the political media either misses entirely… or notices way too late.
The Difference Between Watching Politics and Trading It
By the time election night arrived, the media framing around Texas had basically settled into: “Paxton probably wins.” Which was true.
But prediction markets don’t reward you for being vaguely correct. They reward you for figuring out 
how correct
 consensus actually is. That’s where the opportunity was.
Most traders were still treating the race like a normal competitive primary. Polling averages suggested a relatively comfortable Paxton lead, but still something in the range of a normal political victory. The market mostly agreed.
That’s why the “Paxton by 20+” margin market was sitting around 8%.
And honestly, once you stepped back and looked at the incentives, that number started to feel ridiculous. Because this race stopped being a traditional Senate primary the second Donald Trump endorsed Paxton. That was the real signal.
We’ve talked about this thesis repeatedly on the show: When Trump decides he wants something in a Republican primary, Republican voters usually comply.
Not always. But often enough that the market still seems too slow to fully price it in. The interesting part is that people 
say
 they understand this dynamic. Then they continue pricing races like they 
don’t
. That disconnect is where a lot of these opportunities come from.
The “Sarah Gonzalez Fade”
One of my favorite parts of tonight’s episode was revisiting what we like to call the “Sarah Gonzalez Fade.” There was this weird stretch where the market kept assuming Trump would eventually endorse Cornyn simply because he 
hadn’t endorsed Paxton yet. 
But every day Trump stayed silent, the opposite became more obvious.
If Trump wanted to save Cornyn, why was he waiting? Sarah pointed this out weeks ago on 
Stu Does America
, and in retrospect you can literally watch the market slowly realizing she was right in real time. The chart starts fading. Cornyn starts slipping. Paxton starts climbing. The endorsement eventually lands and suddenly everyone acts shocked by the result the market had already been whispering about for weeks.
That’s the stuff I love. Not just “who wins.” But watching the market slowly absorb reality.
Why the Margin Market Mattered
One thing we dug into tonight that I think newer traders really need to understand: Sometimes the best value is not the winner itself. Sometimes it’s the 
magnitude.
By the time we got close to election night, Paxton outright had already become expensive. The easy value was mostly gone. But the margin markets still looked sleepy.
That’s where the “20+ point win” position came from. And again, this is where politics and math collide in a weirdly beautiful way. A 10-point race sounds massive in political media language. But mathematically? It’s just 55-45. You only need a relatively small shift in voters to suddenly create a giant-looking margin.
Once I started thinking through the Trump endorsement that way, the possibility of a blowout stopped looking crazy. The market still thought it was crazy. That’s why the price existed.
The Bigger Point
One thing I tried to stress on tonight’s show: This is not about “getting lucky” on random moonshot bets. If you come into these markets blindly chasing every low-probability outcome because you want 1000% returns every day, you’re going to get annihilated.
The point is identifying situations where the market probability itself feels fundamentally broken. Sometimes those are 60-cent positions. Sometimes they’re 8-cent positions. The percentage isn’t the story. The mispricing is.
And honestly, that’s what’s been the most fun about building this show with all of you so far.
People in the comments tonight were talking about turning losing streaks around. Paying for dinners. Building vacation money. Starting with five bucks and slowly figuring it out. That’s the ground-floor stuff I love.
Because most people still have no idea this world even exists yet.
Tonight’s episode goes much deeper into all of this, including:
The exact logic behind the Paxton margin position
Why I regretted not going even heavier earlier
Every Texas position we took and how they settled
The “Trump primary thesis” we keep riding
Why politicians are suddenly panicking about prediction markets
And why I think this entire industry is still absurdly early
